The traditional understanding of Digital Manufacturing describes the utilization of a suite of tools to facilitate the integration of product and process design.
The emergence of 'Industrie 4.0' has led to a greater focus on the utilization of real-time data in closed-loop control architectures obtained via ubiquitous sensing and computing.
Additive Manufacturing (AM) is an archetypal process for Digital Manufacturing, as the absence of physical tooling allows the deposition of complex product geometries without many constraints.
AM can efficiently manufacture very small quantities of products, down to a single unit.
The integrated framework for assessing Digital Manufacturing combines a Digital Manufacturing model, a generic AM process map, and a life cycle assessment framework.
The framework describes the Digital Manufacturing workflow as an integrated optimization problem, simultaneously addressing multiple interrelated elements.
Data science techniques, including machine learning, have been used in automated manufacturing for predictive maintenance, demand forecasting, process monitoring, and optimization.
The growing amount of data in a manufacturing environment has turned some existing issues into Big Data problems, requiring an integrated data infrastructure and specialized knowledge.
The integrated framework provides a conceptual basis for the development of integrated approaches to address the complex, interconnected problems in Digital Manufacturing.

Martin Baumers is interested in the economic and operational aspects of Digital Manufacturing technologies, with an emphasis on understanding the total cost, build speed, and energy consumption of 3D Printing/Additive Manufacturing.

Ender Özcan's research interests and activities lie at the interface of Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence, and Operational Research, focusing on intelligent decision support systems combining data science techniques and (hyper/meta)heuristics applied to real-world problems.

The paper discusses how the notion of 'Digital Manufacturing' is transforming from a term describing a suite of software tools to a more general concept incorporating computerized manufacturing, supply chains, and product life cycles.
The paper uses the example of Additive Manufacturing to identify an integrated multi-objective optimization problem underlying Digital Manufacturing.
The paper outlines challenges for the development and application of Machine Learning tools in Digital Manufacturing, including the need for expertise in both data science and optimization.

The paper emphasizes the importance of an integrated data infrastructure and compliance with standards to enable direct communication between data science and optimization techniques in Digital Manufacturing.
